title: The Standard Multiplication Algorithm
short: Multiply multi-digit numbers with stacked partial products.
trouble: Children leave out the placeholder 0 in the second row, so the tens product is worth one tenth of its value.

blocks.html: In Grade 4 you multiplied two-digit numbers with partial products in an area model. The standard algorithm is the same idea written in a compact stack: one row for each digit of the bottom number.
Multiply the top number by the ones digit of the bottom number. Then multiply by the tens digit, starting that row with a 0 because you are multiplying by tens. Add the rows.

In $346 \times 27$, the 2 in 27 is really 20. So the second row is $346 \times 20$, which is $346 \times 2$ tens: $692$ tens, or $6{,}920$. The 0 at the end holds the ones place. The two rows are the two parts of the area model, $346 \times 7$ and $346 \times 20$.

blocks.name: areamodel
blocks.cap: $346 \times 27$ split by place value. The parts in each column add to the rows of the algorithm: $346 \times 20$ and $346 \times 7$.

blocks.html: Leaving out the placeholder 0, so $346 \times 27$ becomes $2{,}422 + 692 = 3{,}114$. That treats the 2 in 27 as 2 instead of 20. Check with an estimate: $350 \times 30$ is about 10,000, so 3,114 is far too small.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 5.NBT.B.5: fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm
